title: This Year's El Niño Is Breaking Records
summary:
Scientists say this year's El Niño is already the strongest ever recorded, based on daily ocean temperatures. It may get even stronger.

An El Niño is a natural climate pattern. It happens when part of the Pacific Ocean near the equator gets warmer than normal. That warm water sends lots of heat into the air. This can change weather around the world, bringing droughts, floods, heat waves and storms.

By September 21, the ocean there was 3.08 degrees Celsius (5.54 degrees Fahrenheit) warmer than average. "It has been a remarkable event," said NOAA scientist Nathaniel Johnson. He thinks it will peak in the next few months.

NOAA has not officially called it a record yet, because it uses a newer way to measure. By that measure, the El Niño of 1997 and 1998 is still stronger, for now.

El Niños usually last about a year. Afterward, an opposite pattern called La Niña often follows.
why_it_matters: A strong El Niño can change the weather where you live, bringing more rain, dry spells or storms.

keywords.explanation: A climate pattern is a change in ocean and air that keeps coming back and affects weather.
The equator is an imaginary line around the middle of Earth.
Droughts are long times with very little rain.
Remarkable means unusual and worth noticing.
The peak is the strongest point of something.
La Niña is the opposite of El Niño, when the same ocean area gets cooler than normal.

Scientists use thermometers on buoys and satellites to measure the ocean's temperature.
